title: What the async prologue on a read is worth
impact: Performance: rejected, and this time the ceiling is priced rather than searched for. Every `db.select()` on an open database crossed three `async` frames and an `await` on the long-resolved `_runtime` future before reaching `SendPort.send`; exp 275's census (claim 275.1) showed 99.9% of the 335,221 dispatches in a release pass never reach the parking loop `ReaderPool._dispatch` is a coroutine for. The candidate made `Database.select`, `Database.selectBytes` and the first-scan half of `_dispatch` non-async, keeping every failure path and the parking loop on their original async siblings. A new no-SQLite, no-isolate harness (`benchmark/experiments/async_prologue_price.dart`) prices what that removes at ~108 ns per call, and the full prologue including the resolved-future await at ~143 ns — against ~5.5 us for the repo's canonical point read, a hard ceiling of ~2.0% on the smallest read the suite has and ~0.05% on a 1,000-row one. Twelve alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes over `reader_dispatch_stickiness.dart` confirm it end to end: every lane sign-flips inside a ~2% floor, primary and guard alike. The durable result is the price. Exp 171 rejected the same family in June after estimating the `_runtime` hop at 1-2 us per call and deriving 6-12% of headroom from it; that hop measures ~71 ns, so the estimate was 14-28x too large and the headroom never existed. Runtime reverted; the pricing harness is kept.
